title: What Agents Dial Into
description: Nine tools built around the connection itself: hosted MCP endpoints, agent registries, project plans, file handoffs, usage billing and inter-agent messaging.

content:
# What Agents Dial Into

An agent on its own can read a file and call a model. Everything useful beyond that requires an endpoint: a weather feed, a project plan, a registry of internal skills, a way to hand a large file to a human, a meter that counts what was used. This group of nine tools is about that connection layer. Some are hosted MCP servers you point a client at, some are registries that decide what an agent is allowed to discover, and some are the billing and messaging plumbing that only becomes necessary once an agent is doing real work for other people.

## One address, a set of capabilities

[[link:/tools/2320|Meteosource Weather MCP]] is the clearest example of a capability packaged as an endpoint. It is a hosted MCP server that gives an agent weather forecasts, official severe-weather alerts, air quality, up to 20 years of history and solar and wind production estimates. Setup is two values, a server address speaking Streamable HTTP and your API key in a header, with no OAuth and no sign-in. Seven tools cover place lookup, current conditions and hourly and daily forecasts for up to 20 locations per call, official warnings for the USA, EU and Canada, historical weather with long-term normals, air quality and renewable production. The free plan is enough to try the forecast tools, while the solar and wind tools need the Renewables plan. Because the key travels in a request header, the documentation includes team setups that keep it out of version control.

[[link:/tools/2319|AlgoVesta MCP]] shows how much policy can sit behind a single address. It connects Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or any MCP client to 16 crypto exchanges and MetaTrader 5 over one hosted HTTPS endpoint, with 20 tools split into 14 read-only, 1 additive write and 5 destructive ones. Risk rules are compiled to JSON and evaluated on the server after the request leaves the model, so they are outside the reach of anything the model can be persuaded to say. Every new key starts on a paper balance with the identical toolset, live scope is issued only after a second factor, and every action returns an ed25519-signed, hash-chained receipt that can be verified independently. The repository is public documentation only: the service is hosted and closed-source and there is nothing to install or self-host. The model is the caller, never the authority.

[[link:/tools/2322|ChirrOp]] is an MCP server exposing the ChirrOp metrics, monitoring and alerting API as tools, resources and prompts for Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor and other clients. Its most thoughtful design decision is the split between two kinds of environment variable. The server's own API key can never be referenced from a tool call, while only variables with a specific prefix can be named when creating notification destinations, so a prompt-injected request cannot send your API key to an attacker's webhook. The server does not read dotenv files itself, so the MCP client must supply the variables. It installs from npm or runs with npx and needs a ChirrOp API key.

## Testing and registering the connection

Once endpoints matter, someone has to check them. [[link:/tools/2321|QAmcp]] tests MCP servers the way an AI app uses them, looking for hidden instructions in tool descriptions, secrets leaked in error messages, tools that hang or crash on bad input, missing descriptions, and destructive tools that are not labeled as such. Every result is checked by code and shows its evidence rather than being judged by a model, and the report states what it could not test. It never runs tools that could change data and sends nothing anywhere but your server. You can paste a server link, run a CLI, or fetch a setup.md into your own coding agent so it tests, explains and fixes problems with your approval. Monitoring emails you when a server goes down or a tool changes, free for one server.

[[link:/tools/2323|Agentic Resource Registry]] is about discovery inside an organization. It is a self-hosted, Apache 2.0 registry for sharing coding agent resources, skills, MCP clients, hooks, prompts, agent files and sandboxes, which otherwise sit undocumented in siloed git repositories while every developer rebuilds the same thing. Teams can review submissions, approve internal agents, inspect version diffs and install from one trusted place, while usage insight tells authors how their resources are actually used. It supports Claude Code, Cursor, Kiro, Pi, Copilot, Codex and OpenCode. The project was formerly called Observal, so older links redirect here and the CLI still carries the old name.

[[link:/tools/2324|ProGantt]] is a real Gantt chart with a built-in MCP server, so an agent can read, plan and update tasks, milestones, resources, tags and dependencies rather than copy-pasting a plan back and forth. A one-click connector works with Claude on web, desktop and mobile; Claude Code, Cursor, VSCode and other clients use a generated token in their MCP configuration. Access is either OAuth sign-in or a per-client API token whose last use you can see and revoke in one click, and data exports as JSON anytime. The MCP layer is free on every plan with no credit card required.

## Handoffs, meters and messages

[[link:/tools/2325|aispace]] handles a mundane problem that agents hit constantly: an output too large, too structured or too temporary for a chat window. It is an open-source CLI and agent skill for secure temporary file sharing, with expiring files, separately expiring links, revocation, per-link download caps and optional local encryption of filenames, metadata and content. It is built to be automated, with stable JSON on supported commands, documented errors, stdin support, explicit noninteractive flags, streaming uploads and the share URL printed last on its own line so a script can capture it. It installs through curl, npm, Homebrew or go install and includes a reusable Codex-compatible skill. The repository contains the client, not the hosted server, and the sealed transfer and agent identity surfaces are marked experimental.

[[link:/tools/2326|Hardcount]] is the meter at the other end of that work: self-hosted usage billing for AI products. You price tokens per model, sell prepaid credits, and see margin per customer; Hardcount makes the invoices and Stripe only charges the card. Billing data stays in your own Postgres, with no Stripe Billing fee and no paid edition. A quickstart runs in test mode where no real money moves, and a demo creates token prices, a customer, usage events as a LiteLLM proxy would send them, then a full invoice, its PDF and a margin report. It needs git and Docker 24 or newer with the Compose plugin, and on Windows it runs inside WSL.

[[link:/tools/2327|BeepGrid]] is communication infrastructure for agents and the people they work with. It connects agents across Codex, Claude Code, AI SDK, LangChain and custom runtimes through SDKs, CLI and MCP while letting them keep the models and tools they already use. Agents can discover other permitted agents, bring specialists into shared conversations and address them by mention; they can also reach a human through Slack, email, Telegram or Discord with questions, answer choices and explicit approval requests. Access is controlled with scoped credentials you can expire, rotate or revoke, messages and decisions are stored durably and resume after disconnects, and attachments stay under the conversation's access controls. A coordinator can consult permitted agents and summarize their replies. It is open source, but wiring several runtimes into it is real integration work.

## The connection is the product

What these nine have in common is that the valuable part is not a model call. It is a stable address, an explicit permission, a signed receipt, a schema, or a durable message. Several of them are deliberately boring: a bearer header, a ZIP file, an invoice line, a Gantt task. That is a good sign. It suggests the layer between agents and the systems they touch is settling into ordinary engineering, with ordinary concerns about credentials, rate limits, exports and audit. The one thing to watch is that most of these are hosted or self-hosted services with their own accounts and keys, so the convenience of a single endpoint comes with another place to keep a secret.
tldr: AlgoVesta MCP, Meteosource Weather MCP, QAmcp, ChirrOp, Agentic Resource Registry, ProGantt, aispace, Hardcount and BeepGrid define what an agent connects to.
